A B S T R A C T

Distributed fiber-optic sensing (DFOS) provides high-resolution, continuous strain measurements along piles, offering new opportunities for detailed assessment of pile quality and soil–structure interaction. However, field DFOS data often exhibit oscillatory patterns traditionally treated as noise, obscuring actual physical insights into variations in pile radius and shaft friction for example. To address this challenge, we propose a numerical framework that formulates the strain-matching problem as a partial differential equation constrained optimization (PDECO) problem. This approach not only infers pile quality and soil response profiles from noisy DFOS data, but also rigorously enforces mechanical equilibrium at each loading step, yielding a physically consistent interpretation of high-resolution distributed measurements.

Numerical benchmarks and application to a DFOS-monitored pile load test demonstrate that the PDECO scheme is robust to measurement noise and capable of reconstructing spatially continuous profiles of pile rigidity, soil stiffness, and shaft friction. Comparisons with independent Thermal Integrity Profiling results further validate the inferred pile radius variations, confirming the method’s effectiveness for detailed pile integrity assessment. Overall, the proposed framework advances pile evaluation by moving beyond traditional layered models and black-box optimization, enabling a more accurate and physically grounded interpretation of DFOS data. Overall, this study establishes a mathematically rigorous approach for high-resolution pile monitoring using distributed sensing technologies.

## 1. Introduction

Compared to traditional strain sensing methods (e.g., vibration wire strain gauge (VWSG)), distributed fiber-optic sensing (DFOS) provides spatially continuous strain measurements along the longitudinal direction of the sensing cable. Specifically, DFOS enables high spatial resolution, ranging from the sub-meter scale with Brillouin Optical Time Domain Analysis (BOTDA) to sub-millimeter resolution with Optical Frequency Domain Reflectometry (OFDR) (Soga and Luo, 2018; Kechavarzi et al., 2019). This capability makes DFOS particularly attractive for pile analysis. Recent studies have employed DFOS in pile sections to evaluate pile–soil interaction and overall pile response (Pelecanos et al., 2018; Beddelee et al., 2022; Ding et al., 2015; Kechavarzi et al., 2019; Kania et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2017).

DFOS-equipped piles typically yield spatially refined and continuous strain fields. A particularly promising application is the use of DFOS measurements to infer soil shaft friction (i.e., the 𝑡–𝑧 curve)

An important next step, therefore, is to invert this process—that is, to directly infer pile radius variations and soil responses with depth from DFOS measurements.

Nevertheless, to the best of our knowledge, no existing method quantitatively relates these oscillations to variations in pile quality. In addition,  existing optimization-based approaches often rely on gradient-free or ‘‘black-box’’ methods. These methods, such as Genetic Algorithms (GA) or Differential Evolution (DE), treat the physical model as an input–output mapping without evaluating or utilizing the gradient of the system. By ignoring the underlying structure of the governing partial differential equations (PDEs), such schemes handle physical constraints only implicitly during the optimization process. Consequently, these ‘‘black-box’’ approaches typically require a vast number of forward PDE evaluations (Pelecanos and Soga, 2018) to navigate the parameter space, leading to significant computational overhead and poor scalability as the resolution of the unknown profile increases.

Technically, this class of problems are widely recognized as inverse problems (Kirsch, 2011; Gosselin et al., 2022; Vogel, 2002; Engl et al., 1996; Tarantola, 2005; Kaipio and Somersalo, 2005). Extensive theoretical formulations and practical applications of this framework are well-established in fields such as geophysical subsurface imaging (Virieux and Operto, 2009), medical tomography (Natterer, 2001; Hansen et al., 2021), and non-destructive defect inspection (Oberai et al., 2003). Unlike gradient-free methods, which are constrained by low computational efficiency and limited to a small number of discrete layer parameters, properly formulated inversion approaches efficiently determine the optimal search direction by embedding the governing PDEs directly into the minimization process.

Leveraging these inversion techniques, this study proposes a numerical scheme to simultaneously infer pile quality and soil response while strictly adhering to the mechanical equilibrium indicated by continuous DFOS strain measurements. The strain-matching problem is formulated as the minimization of a tailored objective function, where the internal mechanical balance of the pile is expressed as a weak-form constraint. This leads to a partial differential equation constrained optimization (PDECO) framework, governed by the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions. By utilizing adjoint-based gradient information, the proposed scheme achieves a convergence rate that is largely independent of the number of parameters, offering a mathematically robust and physically grounded alternative to traditional layered models and black-box optimization.

## 2. Problem statement - axially loaded piles with DFOS measurements

This section formulates an elliptic partial differential equation (PDE) as the governing equation for the mechanical equilibrium of an axially loaded pile, which serves as the primary constraint in the optimization problem. The soil friction effect is modeled using an empirical hyperbolic-type law, with both the tangent stiffness and maximum friction defined as spatially distributed optimization variables. Similarly, irregularities in the pile are characterized by variations in the pile radius or Young’s modulus. At each loading step and time frame, the pile distributed strain measurements are obtained via DFOS. By minimizing the discrepancy between the measured strains and those predicted by the governing equation, the problem is cast into a standard optimization framework. This formulation sets the foundation for the numerical implementation detailed in Section 3.

## 3. Method - PDE constrained optimization

The optimization problem (15) has been widely investigated in the literature (Sun et al., 2020; Beddelee et al., 2023). A common solution strategy involves a trial-and-error matching approach, wherein the PDE constraint (14) is solved repeatedly, and the resulting strain – computed from the mechanical equilibrium – is compared against the DFOS-measured strain.  . Here we provide an intuitive engineering explanation: the problem requires enormous guesses of soil parameters and the pile’s apparent radius to reconstruct a strain profile that matches the dense vertical measurements provided by the sensors. It becomes immediately apparent that this process is non-trivial; achieving an acceptable match between the predicted and measured strain typically requires a high number of iterations to fine-tune the parameter space.

In contrast, this study adopts a variational approach by constructing a Lagrangian functional that incorporates the PDE constraint via an adjoint formulation (Hinze et al., 2008). Specifically, the energy balance principle naturally leads to the mechanical equilibrium equation, which in turn induces the weak form PDE. The adjoint system is then discretized and solved using the Galerkin finite element method (Zienkiewicz and Taylor, 2005).

The problem is further complicated by the nonlinearity and nonhomogeneity of the governing equations. To address this, we apply Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) (Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004) to iteratively determine the search direction in each Newton step. To the best of our knowledge, the resulting system is convex and coercive only under appropriate stabilization. Consequently, this study designs and implements a stabilization scheme that minimally perturbs the original system while ensuring convergence to a physically meaningful solution within an acceptable number of iterations.

Eq. (22) leads to the well-known saddle point problem (Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004; Brezzi, 1974). To ensure good convergence behavior, the inf-sup condition must be satisfied. In simple terms, instability in saddle point systems arises when the number of constraints exceeds the number of degrees of freedom. In this context, the ‘‘number of constraints’’ corresponds to the size of the matrix 𝑨, while the ‘‘number of degrees of freedom’’ corresponds to the size of the matrix 𝑲.

4.5. Performance evaluation

A primary advantage of the proposed PDECO method is its computational efficiency, particularly as the system size increases. In our experience, traditional pile inversion problems, such as those discussed in Pelecanos et al. (2018), Beddelee et al. (2023), suffer from poor scalability; performance often degrades significantly when the number of unknowns exceeds 100, especially when using derivative-free schemes like Genetic Algorithms. This lack of scalability stems from the inability of black-box evolutionary algorithms to exploit the gradient information inherent in the KKT system (20), which could drastically accelerate convergence if properly utilized. To demonstrate this, we conduct a numerical experiment evaluating the scalability of the PDECO scheme across various levels of mesh refinement.

Consequently, multiple tests were performed by varying the number of cells in the vertical direction. Notably, the inclusion of multiple loading steps causes the problem scale to increase substantially. Solving

such a high-dimensional problem with black-box optimization would likely fail to yield a feasible solution within a reasonable timeframe. Using the noise-free configuration detailed in Section 4.1, the PDECO scheme was executed with a constant convergence criterion of 1.0 × 10−11. ## 5. Case study: Pile quality evaluation of an osterberg-cell test in London

In this section, we revisit an Osterberg-cell pile test originally presented in Pelecanos et al. (2018), where the DFOS measurements exhibit suspicious ‘‘wiggling’’ patterns. Traditional methods (Pelecanos et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020) have been unable to explain these patterns while maintaining static equilibrium. The proposed PDECO framework, however, offers a new perspective by attributing the observed irregularities to local variations in the pile radius.

Following the configuration described in Section 5.1, the DFOS data are used as input for the PDECO scheme, while empirically evaluated 𝑡-𝑧 parameters serve as the initial guess for the optimization. To further validate the results, the pile rigidity estimated by PDECO is compared with data obtained from Thermal Integrity Profiling (TIP). This comparison reveals not only qualitative agreement but also aids in interpreting cross-sectional irregularities as apparent radius variations under axial loading.

5.1. DFOS instrumentation

The test pile has a total length of 51 m, with a nominal diameter of 1.5 m and a reinforcement cage diameter of 1.35 m. The cage was assembled in four sections, with O-cells installed in the lowest section, approximately 6 m above the pile base. Therefore, this study focuses on the segment of the pile down to a depth of 45 m. The local stratigraphy

consists of Made Ground overlying the Lambeth Group (sandy silty clay and silty clay), followed by Thanet Sand and Chalk (Fig. 12(a)). The Ocells applied a compressive load to the upper pile segments, eventually reaching a maximum value of 30.87 MN.

The pile was instrumented with DFOS cables, with measurements validated using VWSG, extensometers, and linear vibrating-wire displacement transducers. Four Fujikura strain-sensing cables and four temperature-sensing cables distributed by Excel (Birmingham, UK) were installed outside the reinforcement cage at a radial distance of 0.675 m (Fig. 12(b)). These cables were fixed to the cage prior to concrete casting and were grouped based on their termination depths— either just above the O-cell or at the pile toe. The strain cables were pre-tensioned to approximately 1500–2000 𝜇𝜀. Since this study models the pile as a one-dimensional structure, the average reading from the four DFOS strain cables is used to represent the axial strain profile along the pile for each individual time step.

Strain and temperature measurements were acquired using a Neubrex BOTDR analyzer (Neubrex Co., 2025), with a spatial resolution of 0.5 m, a sampling interval of 0.05 m, and typical noise levels of 20 𝜇𝜀 for strain and 2 ◦C for temperature. BOTDR technology detects shifts in the Brillouin frequency of back-scattered light within the optical fiber, which are proportional to both the mechanical strain and temperature (Soga and Luo, 2018; Rui et al., 2017). To separate these two effects, a gel-filled loose-tube cable mechanically isolated from strain was used for temperature sensing, while the strain-sensing cable directly bonded to the reinforcement cage was used to capture strain. By compensating the strain-cable measurements with the temperature variations obtained from the temperature-sensing cable, pure mechanical strain changes can be accurately determined. Consequently, the optical fiber functions as a distributed sensor, providing continuous profiles of strain ( ̂𝜖 in Eq. (12)), and temperature along the pile.

5.3. Thermal integrity profiling method

Thermal Integrity Profiling (TIP) is a nondestructive integritytesting method that estimates the radius of cast-in-place piles by using the heat of hydration generated during curing and its diffusion to the surrounding ground (Mullins, 2010; Mullins et al., 2007). For TIP analysis, temperature sensors are attached to the reinforcement cage during construction to record temperature–time histories along the pile length. Sections that contain defects such as necking or bulging exhibit changes in both the released hydration heat and the resulting temperature–time response; TIP interprets these variations to estimate the pile’s apparent radius. In common practice, TIP analysis has used discrete temperature sensors installed at intervals along the pile (Sun et al., 2021, 2022). More recently, DFOS has enabled continuous temperature profiling, which supports higher-resolution and more spatially continuous estimates of the apparent radius (Wang et al., 2023; Deng et al., 2021; Zhong et al., 2018; Rui et al., 2017).

In this study, the radius (rigidity) estimated by the proposed PDECO framework was compared with the apparent radius obtained from the TIP analysis conducted at the same test site. Rui et al. (2017) performed the TIP analysis using the temperature cables described in Section 5.1, following the procedure summarized below. Firstly, as illustrated in Fig. 14(a), the temperature–time histories along the pile depth were measured using DFOS cables attached to the reinforcement cage. It should be noted that the total number of datasets was 10,162,112, corresponding to 2603 time frames (at 0.13-hour intervals up to 332 h) and 976 measurement points along the depth at 0.05 m spacing, with four cables in total (2603 × 976 × 4 = 10,162,112). Secondly, as shown in Fig. 14(b), an one-dimensional axisymmetric heat-transfer finite element model was developed to simulate the hydration and heat dissipation process. The heat generation of concrete (𝑞) was defined using the hydration heat model proposed by De Schutter and Taerwe (1995), while the thermal conductivity (𝑘) and volumetric heat capacity (𝜌𝐶𝑝) of the concrete and each soil layer were assigned according to the parameters summarized in Table 4. Third, inverse analyses were performed by varying the pile radius in Fig. 14(b) until the simulated temperature–time curves matched the DFOS-measured data, and the radius producing the best agreement was identified as the apparent radius. Finally, this process was repeated for all depths and for the four temperature cable directions, resulting in the evaluation of the apparent radius profiles for each sensor direction, as presented in Fig. 15.

## 6. Conclusion

This study presents a novel numerical framework for simultaneously inferring pile quality and soil response profiles from distributed fiberoptic sensing measurements on axially loaded piles. By formulating the strain-matching problem as a Partial Differential Equation constrained optimization problem, the approach rigorously enforces mechanical equilibrium while leveraging the high spatial resolution of DFOS data. This framework effectively captures the wiggling strain patterns observed in field measurements, which are linked to the variations in pile radius and soil–structure interaction—phenomena often overlooked or treated as noise in conventional analyses.

Through a number of numerical benchmarks and applications to a real DFOS-monitored pile load test, the PDECO scheme demonstrated robustness to measurement noise and the ability to reconstruct continuous profiles of pile rigidity, soil stiffness, and shaft friction with physical consistency. Comparison with independent Thermal Integrity Profiling (TIP) results further validated the inferred pile radius variations, highlighting the potential of the proposed PDECO scheme for high-fidelity pile quality profiling.

The limitations of the proposed method can be categorized into three main aspects:

First, the mechanical model is based on a one-dimensional pile formulation with a simplified nonlinear soil spring model; consequently, it cannot fully capture three-dimensional soil responses or intricate soil– structure interactions, such as slippage and separation at the pile-soil interface.

Second, while the current soil model utilizes a simplified tangent stiffness with a capacity cap, it could be refined to include hardening or softening effects characteristic of highly plastic soils. Since this study serves as a foundational demonstration of the PDE-constrained optimization framework, we focused on the primary parameters governing pile behavior: stiffness and capacity. Integrating more complex constitutive laws would involve introducing parameters such as a hardening modulus ℎ or degradation factor 𝑑 and deriving the corresponding KKT system. Given the modular nature of the adjoint-based approach, these extensions can be readily incorporated, provided appropriate regularity penalties are applied to ensure inversion stability.
